claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength despite favorable plasticity and machinability.
The starting equimolar CoCrFeNiTi composition corresponds approximately to Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Ti20 in atomic percent.
The relatively low hardness and strength of the starting alloy arise from the absence of nanoscale precipitates or local chemical ordering.
Nanoscale precipitation or local chemical ordering in similar alloys impedes dislocation motion.
In homogeneous untreated CoCrFeNiTi, the absence of nanoscale heterogeneities permits relatively free dislocation motion.
Relatively free dislocation motion produces lower hardness and strength but greater plasticity and machinability.
A controlled aging treatment near 500 °C can induce nanoscale second phases or local chemical ordering in CoCrFeNiTi.
The relevant aging window is approximately 400–600 °C for controlled durations.
The proposed controlled treatment includes aging at approximately 500 °C for 30 minutes to several hours under an inert atmosphere.
Nanoscale precipitates or locally ordered domains formed during aging act as obstacles to dislocation glide.
Obstructing dislocation glide increases resistance to plastic deformation and thereby increases hardness and yield strength.
Aged specimens that develop nanoscale precipitates or local ordering will have greater hardness and yield strength than untreated specimens.
The strengthening caused by aging will be accompanied by reduced ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The controlled comparison is between an as-homogenized solid-solution specimen and a specimen aged at 500 °C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere.
The hypothesis is limited to room-temperature testing, with optional elevated-temperature testing only where additional high-temperature deformation mechanisms are not activated.
Mechanical testing is limited to tensile or compression loading to moderate strains of approximately 5–10%.
Failure to observe a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase together with detectable nanoscale heterogeneities would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the predicted decrease in ductility after aging would falsify the hypothesis.
